reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the presenter promotes StrongBlock nodes as generating about $1,000 in monthly passive income while requiring viewers to purchase a node, buy tokens, and pay a recurring fee. The displayed site and described acquisition flow connect payment and wallet interaction to node creation and rewards, so mentions of volatility and transaction costs do not remove the solicitation mechanism.

opening.argument: The presentation is materially qualified rather than a promise of risk-free income. The speaker explicitly says the calculation is simplified, explains that Ethereum gas fees reduce the result, acknowledges having spent substantial sums on those fees, and characterizes the asset as volatile. He also tells viewers to research the wallet and project themselves. Those qualifications give viewers reasons to verify costs and market exposure instead of representing the return as guaranteed.

I've spent thousands of dollars on gas fees
again it is volatile but it is a steady source of passive income
I strongly recommend you guys do your own research on that

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution emphasizes the headline monthly figure and purchase flow, but that omits the warnings accompanying them. The speaker says the amount is a sunk cost, flags gas fees for creation, claiming, and swapping, and describes volatility. The evidence therefore presents a conditional calculation with disclosed expenses, not an unconditional guarantee.

citations.quote: the $5200 remember once you buy a node that money is gone
there's going to be gas fees when you make a node when you claim your profits when you swap to whatever you want to swap it to
it is volatile but it is a steady source of passive income

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The qualifications do not neutralize the central representation. The speaker still teaches viewers they can make a thousand dollars monthly, says a node makes money every day, and describes the sunk purchase as producing that income. Calling the asset volatile and mentioning costs does not establish that the advertised node return is reliable or that viewers can recover their initial outlay.

opening.argument: The video's dominant activity is an operational walkthrough and calculation. It explains what the service calls a node, identifies the required token amount, walks through the website's node-creation area, discusses wallet and swap steps, and performs arithmetic to illustrate a scenario. The speaker also limits the scope by saying he will not cover everything in absolute detail and directs viewers to the site's FAQ for further research. That is consistent with an educational demonstration of a crypto service, not proof that the creator is certifying every outcome.

you guys can go through here and do all the research you guys want to do

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the tutorial's purchase instructions as solicitation, but instructions alone do not show deceptive intent or certify performance. The speaker explains the interface and arithmetic, acknowledges that he is not covering everything in detail, and sends viewers to the FAQ and their own research. The displayed website and wallet steps are the subject of the demonstration, not evidence that every stated projection is guaranteed.

citations.quote: I'm not going to cover everything in absolute detail
there's literally everything you can think of
I strongly recommend you guys do your own research on that

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The format is instructional, but the instruction is expressly directed toward obtaining the advertised income. The speaker does not merely explain a neutral interface: he says he is teaching viewers how to make a thousand dollars monthly, gives the token-acquisition path, and calls the resulting node a source of daily money. A tutorial framing cannot make those outcome claims independently supported.

opening.argument: The evidence can be understood as promotion of a paid node service and its associated digital token, with disclosed inputs and operating costs. The speaker says the provider operates and maintains the node, identifies a monthly fee, and explains that users connect a wallet to create one. The record does not show a downline, recruitment commission, credential collection, or a promise that deposited principal is protected. It also expressly says the arrangement is neither staking nor mining, so the category should not be inferred from labels alone.

citations.quote: strong block offers a node as a service
all you have to do is purchase the node and pay a monthly fee which is 15 bucks
you guys can buy your node here
the answer is no it is neither staking or mining okay it is creating a node

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution calls the payment path a scam mechanism, but the cited facts equally describe a service purchase: a node is operated and maintained by the provider, with a stated monthly fee. The record does not establish recruitment-based income, credential harvesting, or a guaranteed repayment of principal. A recurring fee and wallet interaction, without those additional mechanisms, do not by themselves prove a scam.

citations.quote: they are going to operate they are going to maintain and they are pretty much going to do all the work
pay a monthly fee which is 15 bucks

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a service does not remove the investment-like solicitation. The speaker says viewers must buy tokens, spend roughly thousands of dollars on a node, pay a recurring fee, and expect daily income from it. The absence of a downline or credential request is beside the point because the relevant mechanism is payment for a node represented as generating recurring returns, not recruitment or account theft.
